This news story changes its main subject in just one day.

The idea was to get back the money the United States spends to keep the strait safe.

Who would collect it, and who would pay it?
What would the 20% apply to?
What currency would be used?
Would there be exemptions?
How would it be enforced?
What would its legal basis be?
No concrete plan for how the system would work was shown.
The fee sign was put up.
But there was still no payment counter or way to calculate it.
That was the situation.
Then, the next day, the scene changed.
Trump announced that he would replace the 20% reimbursement fee plan with trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States.
He explained that the decision was based on “very productive discussions” with Middle Eastern leaders.
The day before, the topic was cargo passing through the strait.
The next day, it was trade and investment with the United States.
It was as if the 20% plan had been put on a different vehicle and sent toward a new destination.
So how did oil prices react?
This is the most interesting part of the news.
After the replacement was announced, Brent crude futures briefly lost part of their rise.
But soon they returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement.
At the time of reporting, they were up about 2.6% from the day before and had passed $85 a barrel.
The story did not simply become: oil would fall because the 20% plan had disappeared.
On July 13, Brent rose 9.59% in one day and settled at $83.30 a barrel.
Reuters linked this rise to a U.S. naval blockade of Iran that was expected to begin the next day, as well as concerns about energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The next day, attacks by the United States and Iran, the naval blockade, and worries about tanker safety continued.
One useful way to see this is not to focus too much on the 20% plan that disappeared.
The plan changed shape the next day, but the question of whether ships could pass safely remained.
A flashy policy post may change its destination, but the tension at sea did not move along with it.
The price movement in this case shows that sudden turn.
Although Trump replaced the 20% Strait fee with investment deals, oil prices stayed high as shipping risks remained.

The 20% Fee Plan Left the Stage.
Crude Oil Prices Did Not.
If you follow only the headlines, the main player changes again and again over two days.
It is as if the script in the oil market had suddenly been rewritten.
Act One came on July 13.
U.S. President Donald Trump posted that all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz should pay a 20 percent fee.
It was a plan to get back the money the United States would spend to keep the strait safe.
Although the 20 percent figure was given, no details were provided, such as who would pay or how the money would be collected.
Even so, Brent crude futures moved sharply on the same day.
They rose $7.29 from the previous day, a 9.59 percent increase.
They settled at $83.30 a barrel.
Here, a major factor separate from the fee plan comes onto the stage.
Reuters linked the rise to the planned U.S. sea blockade of Iran, which was expected to begin the next day, and to concerns about energy shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Then came Act Two on the following day, July 14.
President Trump posted that the 20 percent fee would be replaced by Gulf countries’ trade with and investment in the United States.
The plan to charge 20 percent on cargo was replaced onstage by another plan.
A member of the audience might think: If the fee plan has disappeared, shouldn’t oil prices also fall?
In fact, according to Yahoo Finance, after the announcement, Brent futures briefly gave back some of their gains.
But soon they returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement.
When the article was posted, they were up about 2.6 percent and above $85 a barrel.
However, we cannot say that the 20 percent plan alone caused the rise on the 13th.
On the 14th as well, concerns over attacks by the United States and Iran, the sea blockade, and the safety of tankers continued.
In other words, even though the scene involving the fee plan was rewritten, other factors continued to move on the same stage.
This price movement alone does not fully show how the market judged the 20 percent plan.
All we can confirm is that the rise briefly became smaller after the announcement and then returned to a high level.
Even news about a distant strait is reflected at the same time in the international benchmark for crude oil prices, along with policy statements, military events, and shipping information.
The market movements over these two days teach us not to give a news story just one main player.
Crude oil prices remained high after Trump replaced his 20 percent Hormuz fee plan, as other concerns continued.

Is That Phone Call Really from AI?
Have AI call a store for you.

Wastewater’s Journey Is Changing: From Underground Main Arteries to Behind Homes
Water from toilets and kitchens has two routes through a town.
One route goes through underground pipes to a large treatment plant.
The other route is treated in a septic tank near the home.
In areas with large populations and many homes close together, a public sewer system that collects everyone’s wastewater in pipes is useful.
In a way, it is a main artery running under the town.
But when the population falls, this main artery runs into a problem.
Fewer people use the sewer system, so the fees paid to local governments also fall.
At the same time, the underground pipes and treatment plants grow old.
The cost of repairing or replacing old equipment keeps rising.
The number of passengers is falling, but the cost of repairing the railway is rising.
For a sewer system, this is a very difficult situation.
So a new way of thinking has appeared: instead of using the same method everywhere in a town, choose the route again based on how closely the homes are built.
Public sewers are suitable where homes are close together.
Where homes are spread out, it may be more economical to treat the wastewater at each home than to extend long pipes and connect them to a large plant.

Kitakata City in Fukushima Prefecture reviewed its wastewater treatment plan because the cost of maintaining its aging facilities was rising, while income from user fees was falling as the population decreased.
Areas that are not served by a shared treatment system will become areas for individual treatment using combined-treatment septic tanks.

A combined-treatment septic tank is like a small treatment plant near the home.

In an age of population decline, sewer systems are not disappearing.

To Solve the Mystery of Space Weapons, Start with Their “Address,” Not Their “Capabilities”
When we hear that “weapons have been deployed in space,” it feels as if a huge new weapon has appeared.
But the main point of this news is not how flashy the weapon is.
On September 14, U.S. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said that space-control weapons had been deployed in orbit to protect joint forces from the actions of hostile opponents.
An official U.S. government article recorded this as the first statement acknowledging that the Space Force had deployed weapons into space.
However, we should not start imagining a blueprint right away.
No specific system name or attack ability has been confirmed.
What we know is that the United States has officially acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit.
The details of what these devices are have not been made public.
First, a weapon that can attack satellites and a weapon placed in space are not the same thing.
In 2021, Russia destroyed a satellite with an anti-satellite missile that rose directly from the ground.
This test created more than 1,500 pieces of space debris that could be tracked.
It was a shocking event, but the weapon’s address was on the ground.
That is a different matter from keeping a weapon in orbit.
Next, we come across the term “counterspace.
This term does not refer only to attack weapons.
According to the U.S. Space Force, it is a general term for attacks and defenses carried out in orbit, through communication links, and at ground facilities.
It includes protecting satellite communications, watching what is happening in space, and tracking missiles.
The fact that surveillance or protection is taking place does not, by itself, confirm that an attack weapon has been placed in orbit.
We should also check the rules of the Outer Space Treaty here.
What the treaty clearly bans includes placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth or in outer space.
It does not ban all space weapons.
Based on this statement alone, we cannot decide that the treaty has been violated.
If we rush after flashy words in space news, we can easily get lost.
Is it a test launched from the ground, an activity that includes attacks and defenses, a surveillance task, or a deployment into orbit?
First, check the address, and the true nature of the story becomes clear.
Above the satellites that support location information and communications, the address of weapons is becoming a new point of dispute.
To understand reports of space weapons, first ask where they are located, because their capabilities remain unclear.

Space Weapons Have Addresses.
That Is Where Things Get Complicated
When it comes to weapons in space, it may be easier to understand them by looking at an address book than a list of performance figures.
Are they on the ground, or are they orbiting?
That alone changes the meaning of the same space weapon.

On September 14, 2026, the US secretary of the Air Force acknowledged that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit to protect its joint forces from the actions of hostile opponents.
It was the first time a US government agency had officially acknowledged the Space Force's deployment of weapons in space.
But the details are still hidden.
The thing we know is that it is being deployed in orbit.
This brings us to ground-launched weapons that attack satellites.
In 2021, Russia launched a missile from the ground and destroyed a satellite.
As a result, more than 1,500 pieces of trackable debris were created.
The missile flew into space, but the weapon's address was still the ground.
That is the difference from the deployment in orbit that the United States acknowledged this time.
Also, counterspace, which means operations against space, is not limited to work in outer space.
The stage can be a satellite's orbit, the communications linking satellites and the ground, or facilities on the ground.
You can jam radio signals, launch cyberattacks, or attack facilities on the ground.
There are ways to stop a satellite from working without shooting it directly.
In other words, you can make trouble for space without going into space.
Defense, too, is not only about flashy weapons.
It can mean warning of danger early, making equipment harder to destroy, spreading out its functions, keeping backups, or moving a satellite so that an attack misses.
The US Space Force divides these measures into active defense and passive defense.
There is also an easy-to-miss line in the law.
Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty bans placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit or on celestial bodies.
However, it does not ban all space weapons.
Space security changes depending not only on whether weapons are fired, but also on the weapon's address, where the attack takes place, and how defense is carried out.
Our daily lives, which rely on communications and location information, are not unrelated to that address book.
The key to understanding space weapons is their address: attacks can affect space without entering it.

When you hear, “Space weapons have been deployed,” you may picture a scene from a movie trailer, with attack weapons being placed in space one after another.
But in this news, the names are just as confusing as the weapons themselves.
On September 14, U.S. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit to protect joint forces from hostile forces.
An official article from a U.S. government agency recorded this as the first statement acknowledging that the Space Force had deployed weapons in space.
Up to this point, things are clear.
The United States officially acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit.
That is the main point of this news.
Now, here is a quiz.
If, when you hear “counterspace,” you picture only weapons placed in space, your answer is incomplete.
In the U.S. Space Force’s framework, this term is a name for attacks and defense carried out in orbit, through communication links, and on the ground.

Make equipment harder to damage.
Spread out facilities and functions.
Make them movable.
Keep backups.

It even includes preparing, without using weapons, to make it less likely that an attack will bring everything to a stop.
Of course, active defense can sometimes include weapons.
However, “counterspace” and “space weapons in general” do not mean the same thing.
What was officially acknowledged this time was the deployment of space-control weapons in orbit.
If we expand that into “the United States has deployed all its space weapons,” the scope becomes far too broad.
Before jumping at a flashy headline, look at what is there, where it is, and what it is for.
Reading space news is a little like being a detective.

When you see news about space weapons, do not start by imagining their performance.

Is the weapon in space?

Does it enter communication networks?

In 2021, Russia launched an ASAT, or anti-satellite missile, from the ground and destroyed one of its own satellites.

Satellites that find and track missiles are also described as sensors for defense.
However, active defense may include weapons.

Article IV bans placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth or anywhere in outer space, as well as placing them on the Moon or other celestial bodies.
It also bans military bases and forts on celestial bodies, along with weapons tests and military exercises there.
However, it is not accurate to call it a treaty that completely bans all space weapons.
The main point this time is not that space weapons have suddenly appeared.
It is that the United States has officially admitted for the first time that it is deploying them in orbit.
Is it a ground-based test, a broad military concept, a defensive system, or a weapon banned by the treaty?
